report:
## What the Evidence Shows

The picture on cranberry and recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs) has shifted over time, and the honest answer is "it depends" rather than a flat no.

**Earlier verdict — no clear benefit:** Cochrane's 2012 update concluded cranberry juice was unlikely to prevent UTIs, a finding widely reported (e.g., ScienceDaily's "Cranberry juice now unlikely to prevent cystitis, review finds," https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2012/10/121016204143.htm). Subsequent well-designed trials reinforced skepticism: a 2016 RCT in older women found cranberry capsules no better than placebo (https://www.acsh.org/news/2016/10/29/cranberries-good-dinner-not-so-much-utis-10373), and a noninferiority trial comparing cranberries to antibiotics in premenopausal women found cranberries less effective (https://infeksiyon.org/en/cranberry-for-prevention-of-urinary-tract-infectiontime-to-move-on/).

**Latest update — modest benefit in specific groups:** The most recent Cochrane review (2023, 5th update, 50 trials, ~8,857 participants) reversed course somewhat, finding cranberry products (juice or tablets) reduced symptomatic, culture-confirmed UTIs in women with recurrent UTIs, children, and people with UTI-prone conditions — though the certainty of evidence was rated low-to-moderate and effect sizes were modest (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001321_cranberries-preventing-urinary-tract-infections; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37068952/).

**Bottom line:** The evidence is inconsistent across trials, dependent on product type, dose (especially proanthocyanidin content), and adherence, and effects are generally small. Many individual high-quality RCTs show no benefit, while pooled meta-analyses suggest a modest reduction in recurrence for women specifically. So "no" captures the skepticism warranted by much of the trial evidence, but it's more accurate to say cranberry products offer, at best, a small and uncertain protective effect—not a reliable prevention strategy.
